PEACE BENEATH THE STONE
SAVA · IVARRA · THREE DAYS BEFORE THE FESTIVAL OF RETREAT
For four centuries, Ivarra had known no war. In that peace, everything dangerous had either been removed from the world, moved into a museum, or renamed a procedure.
Sava Ilen woke before the morning signal, both auditory sails raised and her heart racing at a sound she could not locate.
She lay motionless in the sleeping niche. In Ivarra’s homes, the walls were not entirely rigid. The ceramic root from which they had been grown retained a calculated elasticity, so that footsteps, blows and serious faults could be felt through the bones before they reached the ears. The floor was now sending her small, rapid vibrations. Not an alarm. Not a collapse. More like one light object striking another, with a persistence that belonged only to children.
Sava climbed down from the niche and opened the room’s panel.
Nemi stood barefoot in the shared gallery, her festival ribbon hanging over one eye. She was trying to strike the floor three times without her bone toy jumping out of a chalk circle.
“Shadow, shelter, silence,” the little girl said. “But if I strike too slowly, the instructor says the predator hears me between the beats.”
“The predator is a sheet of cloth pulled along a wire.”
“In the drill. In ancient times it was real.”

Oru switched off the projection and looked at her with his whole attention. For a nivar, this meant turning the head almost squarely towards someone and giving up half the field of vision. The gesture could be tender or aggressive. With Oru, it was usually a request that she stop hiding inside her profession.
Nemi looked from one to the other, chewing slowly. Sava did not want the little girl to turn every minor disagreement into a danger signal. She lowered her voice.
Taren agreed to another series. An unexpected bell. A tilting floor. The smell of blood. A silhouette dropping from the ceiling. Each time, his body gave him a moment in which he could look before he became afraid. Each time, the machine called that moment a defect.
They walked towards the central levels. Taren was a head taller than she was, but he still carried something of the child she had pulled through the smoke: a hesitation before coming closer, as though every affectionate gesture first had to be checked for traps.

TAREN AND SAVA · IVARRA · YEAR 412 OF THE LONG QUIET

THE CHAMBER OF MEASURE
SAVA · IVARRA · THE THIRD DAY AFTER THE ATTACK
The Chamber of Measure preserved peace through a simple and impossible arithmetic: each permitted life had to occupy the place of a life ended or a harvest still uncertain.
The Chamber of Measure did not forbid births. It placed them in the future.
That was the official wording and, on most days, Sava managed to believe it. Arua could not be made larger. To the east, living tissue cooked in the open air, and water boiled in the surface fissures. To the west, gases froze in hollows and winds carried needles of solid nitrogen. Between them lay the Belt: a fertile strip seven thousand kilometres long, maintained by orbital mirrors, geothermal channels and a demographic discipline older than every building in Ivarra.
Each family received the right to a first birth. The second depended on deaths, root yields, space available in the depths and the region’s genetic diversity. A third was rare. A fourth existed only in the provinces’ obscene songs.
Nivari generally lived between fifty and sixty standard years and matured quickly. Without predators and restrictions on births, the models showed that the population would double every six years. Within a single lifetime, the Belt would become a hungry mass driven towards fire and ice.

Sava remembered her first day at work. She had been thirteen and was still in mourning for her parents. Her mentor, Lio Marr, had shown her the map of the Belt and told her to look at the red points.
“Each one is someone we say no to,” he had explained. “If we cannot bear that, we’ll say yes to everyone, and in twenty years there will be no one left to say anything to.”
The last applicants of the cycle wore around their necks the black thread of the Whole Hearing, an old tradition from the galleries of the Night. They believed that every birth brought the community a combination of hearing that had never existed before, and that choosing embryos by scores meant closing off part of the world before it could be heard. They had refused the mandatory genetic testing.
His partner had a mutation that could cause complete deafness in one child in six. The Chamber recommended an embryo without the marker. The two wanted random conception.

In the transparent liquid floated a mouth not yet born.

THE LOWER ARCHIVE
SAVA AND TAREN · IVARRA · THE END OF THE WEEK

The Lower Archive did not exist on the public plans. Sava descended in an unmarked lift with two agents of the Quiet. The walls were not grown from root but cast in a grey alloy, technology from the time of the Cleansing.
Seln Aru was waiting beside a transparent tank.
A saryx embryo floated inside.
It was the size of her palm, its wings drawn around its body. A thin cord joined it to a nutrient membrane. THE NIGHT TRAIN
SAVA · THE ROAD BETWEEN IVARRA AND VAOR
The trains towards the edge of the Night had been built to make distance bearable. Passengers spent most of the journey beneath rock and saw the world only when they could no longer get off.
The Night Train left Ivarra without windows.
As far as the border of Vaor, the tunnel followed the safe depth, where rock retained heat and no traveller had to see the surface. Only after thirteen hours did the carriages rise towards the Belt, and their walls become transparent. Beyond them, Arua unfolded like a wound between two infinities.
To the east, the Day was a reddish-white plain beneath shimmering air. To the west, the Night began under a wall of blue clouds, its glaciers faintly reflecting the light of the orbital mirrors. Between them stretched the low forests of mineral ferns, the black channels and the mounds of buried cities. The star Vei never rose or set. It hung at the same height, a red coin driven into the horizon.
The nivari in the carriage instinctively pressed towards the side away from the window. Even after centuries of safety, the open surface quickened their hearts. Sava too felt the impulse to crouch. Taren stood straight, looking at the sky.
“Doesn’t it bother you?” Oru asked.
“What?”
“The fact that there’s no ceiling.”
Taren raised a hand towards the glass.
“There is. It’s just very far away.”
Nemi laughed.
The corridor was crowded. Passengers from the centre kept their luggage close, their sails lowered so as not to touch anyone. In front of the freight carriage, three employees of House Veyr were trying to push back a group of people dressed in work cloth. They wore no passenger wristbands. A woman held a child against her abdomen, and a boy Nemi’s age pressed his sleeve over his mouth and coughed without a sound.
Oru walked past him and opened the freight door. The air inside was damp and heavy. Mesh beds had been stretched between crates of spores, filters and nutrient tubes. Twenty-seven people shared the space reserved, by volume, for sixteen tonnes of equipment. Condensation ran down the walls. An older man was trying to turn a jammed fan by hand.
When the train started again, Kol and the others were allowed to remain in the passenger carriages. The conductor demanded Sava’s signature for the deviation. She signed and added the actual number of people. The system immediately flagged the discrepancy with the manifest.
She stopped. In the compartment, Kol had fallen asleep with Nemi’s container in his arms. The woman from Vel Four had covered him with her own cloak. If Sava continued, the train could be stopped at the next node and the people sent back to a place without a harvest. If she did not, their transport remained legal only because they had not been considered people.

THE SECOND VAOR
TAREN · VAOR · THE FIRST WEEK
The “second Vaor” appeared on no map. Yet it had midwives, markets, rules of neighbourliness, debts, songs and dead — all the things through which a crowd becomes a city before the state grants it a name.
The young woman’s name was Vessa Dahr, and she was a doctor only because no one else had agreed to care for the hidden settlements. She led them through a gallery concealed by insulation panels. Beyond it, beneath the agricultural chambers declared abandoned, stretched a second Vaor.
There were no squares, schools or separate dwellings there. Families slept in niches dug between the supply roots. Children ran naked through the warm steam, so many that the floor vibrated continuously beneath their footsteps. Sava reflexively counted the first twenty small bodies, then gave up. Every adult carried the scent of more relatives than any legal file allowed.
“How many?” she asked.
Vessa pulled off her gloves, stained with the animal’s blood.
“Here, eleven thousand. In all the chambers, perhaps eighty thousand.”
“The model indicates more.”
“The model includes glassbacks. They like the nutrient mixture for newborns.”

“Daran knows as much as it is useful for him to know.”

The workers’ meal continued long after the bowls were empty. Not because they had extra food, but because each vessel had to be rinsed in the same water, which was then poured into a crop tank. In Ivarra, cleaning made things disappear. Here, nothing disappeared; it simply passed into another use.
Bes led them into a side gallery where his family shared three niches with two other families. There was no door. A fibre curtain separated the space from passers-by, and plaques bearing names, debts and care shifts hung on the wall. Sava counted without meaning to: seven adults, twelve children, two visible pregnancies and an old man whose breathing had a wet wheeze.

The verses listed the names of galleries, springs and places where the root was thick enough to withstand a collapse. It sounded like a lullaby. It was also an evacuation map. Seln's trial was meant to separate the old order from the new. Instead, it showed how many instruments of centralised peace had become indispensable to the very people who defeated it.
Seln Aru's trial lasted nine months and produced six incompatible definitions of peace.
Central agents maintained that veyrin had prevented a lethal attack. Vaor's survivors showed the bodies of those who had died too calm to run.
